input.question: When it is silent, why does the ticking of a clock change pitch?
input.ground_truth: It's a psychological effect in our constant attempts to find patterns in things. If you try to switch the ticks and tocks you would be able to. Except for minute differences in the gears leading to small pitch differences, the pitch is usually identical.

Okay, let’s imagine the clock is like a little bird that goes "tick-tock, tick-tock" to help us know the time.

When the room is quiet, there aren’t any other sounds around to cover up the clock’s little "tick-tock" noises. So, we can hear them very clearly, like how you can hear your friend whisper when everyone else is being super quiet.

Sometimes, the "tick" sound might seem to change a little—like it sounds higher or lower. That can happen if the clock is very old, or if the air around it changes a bit (like if it gets a little warmer or cooler). But mostly, when it’s silent, you just notice the clock’s sound more because there’s nothing else to listen to!

So, the ticking doesn’t really change pitch all by itself—it’s just that in the quiet, you hear it better!
